source.title: Refit the Probe: Single-Direction Ablation Is Not a Necessity Test

record.tranche_reason: The paper argues that single-direction probe ablation is not a necessity test, but its experiments use formal sequence-task state variables in small models and fine-tuned pretrained models, not safety-trained chat models or refusal. It does not test or use any of the listed refusal-claim versions.
record.gate_note: No harmful or harmless instruction prompts, refusal measurements, or safety-trained chat-model experiments are reported. The paper tests probe-direction ablation and refitting on formal-task states; these analogous method findings are recorded under fits_no_version. The paper also reports iterative nullspace erasure, but that tests a different intervention and task variable, not the listed refusal versions.
record.test_reason: The paper studies logistic-probe directions for formal sequence-task state variables (Parity, S3, Dyck depth) in small task-trained models and fine-tuned Pythia/Mamba. It has no harmful/harmless prompts, no refusal measurement, and no safety-trained chat models. Its critique of single-direction ablation as a necessity test is general methodology and never mentions refusal. It neither tests nor uses any refusal-direction version.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors argue that single-direction probe ablation does not remove the target, because a refitted probe recovers it. They conclude the ablation's drops cannot support necessity claims either way. Iterative nullspace erasure scored against matched random subspaces shows the readable formal-task representations are load-bearing. Probe-peak and ablation-peak layers differ in every pretrained model they ran.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies logistic-regression probe directions on formal sequence-task states, not a harmful-minus-harmless activation-difference direction. Its principal necessity intervention is iterative nullspace projection, with formal-task accuracy as the outcome.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that layer choice can change single-direction ablation drops, especially across tied probe-accuracy layers; pretrained Dyck ablation peaks occur below probe-accuracy peaks. It also notes that tensor choice and probe-direction variance affect interpretation.

fits_no_version.finding: Refitting a linear probe after single-direction ablation recovers near-original accuracy in nearly all formal-task cells. This holds even after the full K-1 probe row space is removed.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In formal sequence-task models, projecting out one probe direction leaves the probed variable linearly readable, so the ablation drop does not test necessity.

fits_no_version.finding: Single-direction ablation drops depend on layer. In pretrained Dyck models they peak below the layer of peak probe accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For these formal-task models, single-direction fragility and linear readability peak at different layers.

fits_no_version.finding: Iterative nullspace erasure costs 0.78-0.98 relative accuracy where matched random subspaces cost under 0.04. Rank-1 drops on Parity/S3 were 0-4.9%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For formal-task state variables, multi-direction subspace erasure reveals necessity that single-direction ablation misses.

record.code_released: Analysis scripts and per-cell data are available from the author; no URL stated.
record.problems: The experiments do not use refusal or safety-trained chat models, so they cannot establish whether the refusal claim holds. The authors report substantial cross-seed spread in some ablation results and state that pretrained-scale subspace erasure is partial in most cells.
record.rows_left_out: Not extracted: iterative nullspace-projection/subspace-erasure results in Section 7 and Tables 1 and 5, since they concern a different intervention on formal-task state variables rather than the listed refusal versions. Also not extracted: other single-direction task results not needed to show the paper's stated refit and layer-dependence findings.

untested.parts: All: no difference-in-means harmful-minus-harmless direction, no refusal removal or induction, no capability check in chat models.
All: no weight-edit abliteration of released models.
All: no jailbreaks or adversarial training against ablation.
All: refusal geometry not studied. Multi-direction findings concern formal-task variables only.

record.verdict_notes: There is a methodological parallel to V4: refusal could survive outside a single ablated direction. However, the paper reports no refusal or safety-model results, so no verdict can be given. The subspace-erasure results were omitted from the rows, which is acceptable because they bear on no version. Researchers interested in V1/V4 critiques may still find the refit check relevant as a methods caution.

versions.untested_parts: Difference-in-means harmful-minus-harmless direction, refusal removal or induction, safety-trained chat models, and preservation of other abilities.
Weight-edit ablation and refusal in released models.
Jailbreak suppression of a refusal direction and robustness training against its ablation.
Whether refusal is encoded by an affine set, cone, or multiple directions.
Separate encoding of harmfulness judgment and refusal decision.
Transfer across languages, model variants, or base-to-instruct models.
How refusal training affects whether a removable direction exists.

rows.subject: 15 formal-task cells (architectures and tasks not itemized for this aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Refit a linear probe on activations after ablating the original probe direction
rows.measure: Refitted probe accuracy relative to its pre-ablation accuracy
rows.value: 58 of 60 cell-seeds were within 0.02 of where they started
rows.note: Aggregate statement; the paper says both exceptions were Parity Mamba seeds, one substantially.
rows.check: Formal-task probe refit, not refusal. Linked correctly to none. The 58/60 figure comes from the erasure run's first step (Section 6, Fig. 1a).
